frameworks.name: Nail It Before You Scale It
frameworks.definition: Optimize a business model fully in existing location(s) before expanding to new locations; premature scaling adds complexity that is difficult to reverse.

frameworks.name: Rowboat vs Titanic Decision-Making
frameworks.definition: Early-stage businesses should remain as lean and maneuverable (rowboat) as possible before expanding; additional locations create organizational inertia (Titanic) that slows pivoting and decision velocity.

claims.text: For in-home therapy and brick-and-mortar service businesses at ~$40K/month revenue spread across multiple locations, the binding constraint is profit per location, not total revenue volume. Before expanding to additional locations, optimize the business model (product stack, customer journey, delivery format, pricing) in existing locations to maximize revenue and margin per customer.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Initial revenue per location below market-clearing (~$6k+/month per location)
claims.mechanism: Scaling an unoptimized model forces subsequent locations to inherit the same suboptimal structure; retrofitting is expensive once teams are trained and systems are embedded.
bounded_by: Does not apply to software or fully-digital businesses where location is irrelevant
Does not apply to businesses that have already optimized profitability per location

claims.text: The complete customer journey—first product, second product, third product—must be mapped and optimized in each location before scaling. Without this mapping, adding new locations forces expensive retrofitting of training and processes that are already embedded in existing locations.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Once staff are hired and trained on a particular customer journey, changing that sequence becomes organizationally expensive; optimizing first reduces downstream friction.
bounded_by: Does not apply to fully automated workflows

claims.text: Businesses operating multiple locations should maintain maximum leanness and organizational simplicity during the decision-making phase; additional locations increase organizational inertia and reduce decision velocity. A single location (rowboat) allows rapid pivoting; multiple locations (Titanic) make course correction slow and costly.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Organizational complexity from additional locations reduces founder's ability to perceive and respond to market signals; decisions made by the Titanic metaphor take longer to implement because they require coordination across multiple independent units.
bounded_by: Once model is locked in, multiple locations become strategic assets
Does not apply to businesses where each location operates independently with no need for coordination

claims.text: Four levers resolve capacity constraints in scaling service businesses: raising price, adjusting delivery ratio (shorter/denser sessions), productizing the offering, or hiring additional staff. The choice of which lever to deploy depends on team bandwidth and current bottleneck.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Model already established in at least one location
claims.mechanism: Each lever targets a different dimension of the constraint: price increases per-customer value and per-hour economics; delivery compression increases throughput; productization replaces custom delivery with repeatable systems; hiring spreads load.
bounded_by: Levers require different preconditions (price requires brand moat; hiring requires scalable processes)

examples.text: A 10-stage roadmap from zero to $100M+ exists, broken down by headcount stage and by eight business functions: each stage has defined constraints, symptoms, and graduation steps. Alex Hormozi has implemented this roadmap multiple times across software, physical products, service businesses, and brick-and-mortar operations. The roadmap is offered free via acquisition.com/roadmap.

practices.text: Focus on increasing revenue and profit per location before expanding to new geographic markets.
Map the complete customer journey (first, second, third product/upsell) and optimize each step before hiring teams for new locations.
Keep the organization as lean and simple as possible during the model-optimization phase to maintain decision velocity.
